title: A Plain Guide to the National Debt
standfirst: How big it is, who holds it, and why the interest matters.
body: The national debt is one of those figures that is quoted often and explained rarely. It is very large, it keeps growing, and it is easy to feel that it must matter without being quite sure why.
## Debt and deficit are different things

The deficit is the gap in a single year between what the government spends and what it raises in taxes. The debt is the total built up over many years of deficits. When the government runs a deficit, the debt grows. Even a smaller deficit still adds to the pile.

Most of the debt is in the form of bonds, called gilts, which the government sells to raise money. They are bought by pension funds, insurance companies, banks, overseas investors and, in recent years, the Bank of England itself. If you have a workplace pension, there is a good chance part of it is lent to the government.

For years, interest rates were so low that a large debt was cheap to carry. That has changed. When rates rise, new borrowing costs more, and so does some existing debt, especially bonds whose payments are linked to inflation.

Money spent on debt interest is money not spent on hospitals, schools or defence. That is the real cost of the debt for most people: not a bill that arrives one day, but a steady pressure on everything else the government wants to do.

Economists disagree on how much debt is too much. What most agree on is that the direction matters. A debt that keeps rising faster than the economy grows leaves less room to respond the next time a crisis hits.
